en: Was angered and enraged,
While the racehorse beneath him,
Circling like a blue vulture,
With jezail gun and steel-tipped arrow,
Kojo girded himself once more,
He was about to trace the line,
Upon Semetey's head
He meant to work a marvel.
He meant to aggravate the wound,
Upon Semetey's head
He meant to bring calamity.
He meant to burn his heart,
Upon Semetey's head
Your Kojo meant to wreak
Havoc no man could wreak.
He meant to begin the mischief,
Fighting as he flew;
May the wretched Kojo never prosper,
He meant to work a marvel.
Low mist shimmered over the earth,
And mingling with the low mist,
Kojo drew near.
Supremely ready for combat,
From the beginning, in combat,
He was a plainly proven great master.
Drawing near within the mist,
He came within half a target's range,
And saw upon the orphan son of Manas
The place at which to aim.
Seeing it, he took delight,
And now began his mischief.
With a gaping steel-tipped arrow,
At Semetey's head
Hero Kojo began his assault.
Snatching up his arrows,
He turned and drew the bow,
And from where he stood, at Semey,
He loosed six thousand shots.
With steel-tipped arrows at his shoulder,
Chynkojo snatched them up,
And shot a thousand with those.
The fiery Oroybo matchlock,
Chynkojo snatched it up,
And fired a hundred with it.
Poor Kojo then
Drew his bow like pouring rain,
And fired bullets like hail.
Semetey was hard beset;
Had his helmet not been iron,
His fur cap would have been shattered.
The sable cap upon his head
Had been turned into a sieve,
But his coat of mail and helmet,
Those two had stopped the shots.
Had those two not been there,
Chynkojo, son of Shygai,
Upon Semetey's head
Would have brought the end of days.
Made of blue-green cloth,
The great saddlebag Kanykei had made,
A green-blue saddlebag in hue,
No camel's load, but a bull-camel's saddlebag,
Upon the noble Buurul
Was always carried.
Your bloodthirsty hero's ammunition
Was powder unmatched among the people.
That saddlebag held a marvel,
With powder filling its inside.
Powder on one side, bullets on the other—
There was no such wonder in the world.
Among those who fought while flying,
There was no villain like Chynkojo.
Hero Semey, the son of Manas,
Your hero born wise.
His bullets flew apart through the sky and reached him,
Yet his entire body
Went on without stirring,
With ringing impacts, he paid no heed,
And the bullets raining down
He valued no more than his trouser cuff.
Heroic courage and lionheartedness
Allah Most High, withholding nothing,
Had bestowed on him beyond measure.
He opened the ammunition pouch,
In desperate need then,
And scattered shots into the sky.
This was why he scattered them:
Chynkojo could not be seen,
So he fired toward an unknown place.
At the edge of a swirling cloud,
Semey fired a hundred shots,
And shot away the mane and tail
Of Chynkojo's Black Horse.
As if he would leave no humiliation unpaid,
The crouching lion
Seemed about to seize Kojo.
Upon Buurul beneath him,
He lashed from side to side,
Spurring right and left,
Your mighty prince grew ardent,
And raged like a lion.
They exchanged fire, sparing no life,
They exchanged fire in furious assault.
The Buurul horse ran without stopping,
Crossing rounded mountains,
Passing many bulging valleys,
One in the sky and one on earth,
They stood their ground, sparing no life,
And the two gray wolves fought.
The ammunition in the saddlebag
Had all been shaken out,
And Semetey, the son of Manas,
Despaired of his doomed life.
The powder shook out of the powder flask,
And he despaired of his anguished life.
There was no bullet in his cartridge pouch,
And your mighty prince and sultan
Had no ammunition together.
Black within and fiery without,
There was no one who knew his secret.
His greatness was beyond compare;
As he went on fighting,
There was no companion here
To bring him ammunition.
When the gray wolf stood hemmed in,
When he turned Buurul's head,
Chynkojo, son of Shygai,
Kojo whose deeds were formidable,
Drew his bow like pouring rain,
And fired bullets like hail.
Black mist billowed from the sky,
His bullets screamed through the air,
A thousand at a time he fired and passed,
A hundred at a time he fired and passed,
Then the Alengir bow and steel-tipped arrows,
With those he shot forty times;
Chynkojo had begun the battle,
And went on thus without regret.
In his bow and gun
Not half a shot remained.
He pondered and spoke,
And devised every grave calamity.
Chynkojo, son of Shygai,
Kojo whose deeds were formidable.
Then Kojo thought this,
Kojo, a hero clear in mind,
Conceived an evil no man could know:
“If I descend and fight on earth,
Semetey the swine will spare no life.
I shall turn back,
I shall go to Jeti-Özön.
Beside Jerge-Tal,
I have a sufficient treasury.
Taking bullets from the treasury,
Taking abundant ammunition,
From the fugitives who fled and escaped
I shall gather an army again,
Taking all the army in abundance,
Upon the head of the bloodthirsty son of Manas
I shall bring down a fog of calamity,
And from the black-hearted bloodthirsty one
I shall take my vengeance at last.
Dragging him along the road,
I shall expose him to the Dangyt.
Making my gray-wolf nature known,
Sending the arrogant one into the grave,
I shall slaughter much of his people,
And that accursed fugitive,
Together with his slaves, all at once,
I shall destroy, and only then rest.
I shall plunder all he owns,
Thus shall I wreak the mischief.
The bloodthirsty one who came raging,
I shall utterly finish.”
Turning back and crying “Chu!”
Chynkojo departed in wrath;
Abandoning the struggle then,
Chynkojo went to his city.
To take abundant ammunition,
Chynkojo went away.
To bring calamity upon your mighty one,
Chynkojo went away.
Let us leave him there,
And begin the news of
The lion prince Semetey.
The Ak-Olpok upon him,
The coat your fierce heroic mother
Had made firm, could be seen.
Whenever the lion moved,
From atop Ak-Olpok
Bullets poured like hail.
When he saw Kojo's bullets,
The prince's heart was shaken;
Jezail bullets and bow-shafts,
Whenever he moved then,
Spilled to the ground like rain.
“If Chynkojo turns and comes back,
I despair of my precious life;
The end of days will appear.”
God's sun in heaven was overcast,
And upon the lone lion of his father
Sixty worries came at once.
The bullet's blow had struck hard,
Striking deep into his breastbone;
When he cried, “Oh!” from his mouth
Blood gushed out in spurts.
His strength left him, his insides burned,
And power departed from your lion.
If the moon is darkened by the sun,
That is what the night is like, he thought;
When its light comes,
That is what the day is like, he thought.
In anger his words came to an end,
He despaired of his precious life,
And grief smoldered deep within him.
There was no steed to ride into battle,
No kinsman to hear his last testament.
“What will the day bring?” he thought;
There was no forest into which to flee,
No Nogai to serve as his support.
My being a hero is beyond compare,
But when I bowed, the one who found counsel,
Dear Bakai, was not here.
Before the mountain-like Kojo,
It seems I shall come to grief.
I shall die an unclean death,
A feast for crow and raven.
With no man and no people,
It seems I shall remain on the mountain pass.
Clutching Buurul and grieving,
It seems I shall remain in the desert.
Strength left the Buurul horse,
And from the mouth of lion prince Semey
Black blood flowed.
The bullet's blow had struck hard,
His whole body grew numb,
He stood looking dazed;
The forlorn Ak-Kelte
Had no bullet for a single shot,
God had struck him in this way.
When he turned Arbuudan’s head,
The lion prince then
Stood sunk in grief.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Had cares too many for his breast:
“Where has my gray wolf gone?” he cried,
Tears from his eyes flooding ten plains.
His face paled and grew thin;
Tears flowing from both eyes
Poured down over his breast.
“If I am parted from my khan and uncle,
To what grave shall I go?” he cried.
“My leopard prince and uncle—
Where can I find him?” he cried.
His breast could not hold his many cares;
Until he found his gray wolf,
